content.prompt: Determine whether the following are geometric sequences.

answer.worked: $$\frac{6}{2}=\frac{18}{6}=\frac{54}{18}=\frac{162}{54}=3.$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=3$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{100}{1000}&=\frac{10}{100}=\frac{1}{10}\\\frac{1}{10}&=\frac{0.1}{1}.\end{aligned}$$Every consecutive-term ratio is $\frac{1}{10}$, so the sequence is geometric.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{-2}{1}&=\frac{4}{-2}=\frac{-8}{4}=-2\\\frac{16}{-8}&=\frac{-32}{16}=-2.\end{aligned}$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=-2$.
$$\frac{5}{2}\ne\frac{10}{5}=2.$$The consecutive-term ratios are not constant, so the sequence is not geometric.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2}&=\sqrt{2}\\\frac{4}{2\sqrt{2}}&=\sqrt{2}\\\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{4}&=\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=\sqrt{2}$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\div\frac{1}{2}&=\frac{1}{5}\times2=\frac{2}{5}\\\frac{2}{25}\div\frac{1}{5}&=\frac{2}{25}\times5=\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}$$The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r=\frac{2}{5}$.

content.prompt:
Find the ratios $\dfrac{a_2}{a_1}$ and $\dfrac{a_3}{a_2}$ for each sequence to test whether it is a GP.

If the sequence is a GP, write down the first term $a$ and the common ratio $r$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{8}{4}=2\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{16}{8}=2\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=4$ and $r=2$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{8}{16}=\frac12\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{4}{8}=\frac12\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=16$ and $r=\frac12$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{4}{2}=2\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{6}{4}=\frac32\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are different, so it is not a GP.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{-100}{-1000}=\frac1{10}\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{-10}{-100}=\frac1{10}\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=-1000$ and $r=\frac1{10}$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{40}{-80}=-\frac12\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{-20}{40}=-\frac12\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=-80$ and $r=-\frac12$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{29}{29}=1\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{29}{29}=1\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=29$ and $r=1$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{4}{1}=4\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are different, so it is not a GP.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{14}{-14}=-1\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{-14}{14}=-1\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=-14$ and $r=-1$.

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a_2}{a_1}&=\frac{1}{6}\\\frac{a_3}{a_2}&=\frac{\frac16}{1}=\frac16\end{aligned}$$
The ratios are equal, so it is a GP with $a=6$ and $r=\frac16$.

content.prompt: A piece of paper $0.1$ mm thick is folded successively $100$ times. How thick is it now? Give an exact answer in millimetres and an approximation in kilometres to 3 significant figures.

answer.worked:
Each fold doubles the thickness. Including the initial thickness, the geometric sequence has $a=0.1$, $r=2$ and $101$ terms.
$$\begin{align*}a_{101}&=ar^{100}\\a_{101}&=0.1\times2^{100}\\a_{101}&=\frac{2^{100}}{10}\text{ mm}.\end{align*}$$
Since $1\text{ km}=10^6\text{ mm}$, the thickness is
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2^{100}}{10\times10^6}\text{ km}&=\frac{2^{100}}{10^7}\text{ km}\\&\approx1.27\times10^{23}\text{ km}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A principal $P$ dollars is invested at 7% per annum compound interest. Let $A_n$ be the total amount at the end of $n$ years.

answer.worked:
The first term is $a=1.07P$ and the common ratio is $r=1.07$.
$$\begin{align*}A_n&=ar^{n-1}\\A_n&=(1.07P)(1.07)^{n-1}\\A_n&=P(1.07)^n\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use trial-and-error on the calculator to find how many full years it will take for the amount to double, and how many years it will take for it to exceed ten times the original principal.

answer.short: 11 years to double; 35 years to exceed ten times the original principal.
answer.worked:
To double, require $A_n\ge2P$, so $(1.07)^n\ge2$. Calculator trials give
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^{10}&\approx1.9672<2\\(1.07)^{11}&\approx2.1049>2\end{align*}$$
The first full year is 11.

To exceed ten times the principal, require $A_n>10P$, so $(1.07)^n>10$. Calculator trials give
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^{34}&\approx9.9781<10\\(1.07)^{35}&\approx10.6766>10\end{align*}$$
The first full year is 35.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Use logarithms to confirm your answer.

answer.short: Doubling requires $n\ge\log_{1.07}2\approx10.24$, giving 11 years. Exceeding ten times the principal requires $n>\log_{1.07}10\approx34.03$, giving 35 years.
answer.worked:
For doubling:
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^n&\ge2\\n&\ge\log_{1.07}2\\\log_{1.07}2&\approx10.24\end{align*}$$
The least whole number of years is 11.

For exceeding ten times the principal:
$$\begin{align*}(1.07)^n&>10\\n&>\log_{1.07}10\\\log_{1.07}10&\approx34.03\end{align*}$$
The least whole number of years is 35.

content.prompt: A car originally costs $\$20000$, then at the end of every year, it is worth only 80% of what it was worth a year before. Let $W_n$ be its worth at the end of $n$ years.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write down expressions for $W_1$, $W_2$ and $W_3$, and find a formula for $W_n$.

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned}W_1&=20000\times0.8\\W_2&=20000(0.8)^2\\W_3&=20000(0.8)^3\end{aligned}$

This is a GP with $a=20000\times0.8$ and $r=0.8$.

$\begin{aligned}W_n&=ar^{n-1}\\&=(20000\times0.8)(0.8)^{n-1}\\&=20000(0.8)^n\end{aligned}$

$W_n$ is measured in dollars.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use trial-and-error on the calculator to find how many complete years it takes for the value to fall below $\$2000$.

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned}20000(0.8)^n&<2000\\(0.8)^n&<0.1\end{aligned}$

By trial and error:

$\begin{aligned}W_{10}&=20000(0.8)^{10}\approx\$2147.48\\W_{11}&=20000(0.8)^{11}\approx\$1717.99\end{aligned}$

The value first falls below $\$2000$ after 11 complete years.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use logarithms to solve part (b). When you log both sides, if the base of the logarithm is between 0 and 1, you must reverse the inequality.

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned}(0.8)^n&<0.1\\n&>\log_{0.8}0.1\\n&>10.31885\ldots\end{aligned}$

The inequality reverses because the logarithm has base $0.8$, between 0 and 1. The least whole number satisfying this is $n=11$, so it takes 11 complete years.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}a_n&=ar^{n-1}\\a_n&=7\times2^{n-1}\end{align*}$$
For terms less than $70000$:
$$\begin{align*}7\times2^{n-1}&<70000\\2^{n-1}&<10000\\n-1&<\log_2 10000\\n&<\log_2 10000+1\\n&<14.29\ldots\end{align*}$$
Since $n$ is a positive integer, $n=1,2,\ldots,14$. Therefore $14$ terms are less than $70000$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Prove that the sum $S_n$ of the first $n$ terms is always $7$ less than the $(n+1)$th term.

answer.worked:
We need to show that $a_{n+1}-7=S_n$. From part a, $S_n=7(2^n-1)$.
$$\begin{align*}a_{n+1}-7&=(7\times2^n)-7\\a_{n+1}-7&=7(2^n-1)\\a_{n+1}-7&=S_n\end{align*}$$
Therefore $S_n=a_{n+1}-7$, as required.

answer.worked:
For $x\neq1$, the series $1+x+x^2+x^3+x^4$ has $5$ terms, first term $1$ and common ratio $x$, so
$$1+x+x^2+x^3+x^4=\frac{x^5-1}{x-1}.$$
Hence, for $x\ne1$,
$$\frac{x^5-1}{x-1}=1+x+x^2+x^3+x^4,$$
and
$$\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^5-1}{x-1}=\lim_{x\to1}(1+x+x^2+x^3+x^4)=1+1+1+1+1=5.$$

answer.worked:
Let $T$ be the total downloads in the first 20 days.
$$\begin{aligned}T&=2^1+1+2^2+2+\cdots+2^{20}+20\\T&=\underbrace{2^1+2^2+\cdots+2^{20}}_{\text{GP: }a=2,\ r=2}+\underbrace{1+2+\cdots+20}_{\text{AP: }a=1,\ d=1}\\T&=\frac{2(2^{20}-1)}{2-1}+\frac{20}{2}(1+20)\\T&=2\,097\,150+210\\T&=2\,097\,360\end{aligned}$$
The total is $2\,097\,360$ downloads.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that in the 10th year, Kim's annual salary is higher than Alex's annual salary.

answer.short: Kim earns $\$46{,}539.85$ and Alex earns $\$46{,}500$ in the 10th year, so Kim's annual salary is higher.
answer.worked:
Let $K_n$ and $A_n$ be Kim's and Alex's annual salaries in year $n$, respectively.

For Kim, $a=30{,}000$ and $r=1.05$.
$$\begin{align*}K_{10}&=ar^9\\K_{10}&=30{,}000(1.05)^9\\K_{10}&\approx\$46{,}539.85\end{align*}$$
For Alex, $a=33{,}000$ and $d=1500$.
$$\begin{align*}A_{10}&=a+9d\\A_{10}&=33{,}000+9(1500)\\A_{10}&=\$46{,}500\end{align*}$$
Therefore $K_{10}>A_{10}$, as required.

children.label: b
children.prompt: In the first 10 years how much, in total, does Kim earn?

answer.worked:
Kim's annual salaries form a geometric sequence with $a=30{,}000$ and $r=1.05$.
$$\begin{align*}S_n&=\frac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}\\S_{10}&=30{,}000\left(\frac{1.05^{10}-1}{1.05-1}\right)\\S_{10}&\approx\$377{,}336.78\end{align*}$$

children.prompt:

How many years does it take her to save $\$87{,}500$?

answer.worked:
Alex's annual savings are $11{,}000,\ 11{,}500,\ 12{,}000,\ldots$ dollars, an arithmetic sequence with $a=11{,}000$ and $d=500$.

Find $n$ such that $S_n=87{,}500$.
$$\begin{align*}S_n&=\frac n2[2a+(n-1)d]\\87{,}500&=\frac n2[22{,}000+(n-1)500]\\87{,}500&=\frac n2[21{,}500+500n]\\250n^2+10{,}750n-87{,}500&=0\\n^2+43n-350&=0\\(n-7)(n+50)&=0\\n&=7\quad\text{or}\quad n=-50\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
An eight-sided die is marked with numbers $1, 2, \dots, 8$.
A game is played by rolling the die until an $8$ appears on the uppermost face.
At this point the game ends.

children.label: i
children.prompt:
Using a tree diagram, or otherwise, explain why the probability of the game ending before the fourth roll is
$$\frac{1}{8} + \frac{7}{8} \times \frac{1}{8} + \left(\frac{7}{8}\right)^2 \times \frac{1}{8}$$

answer.short: The game ends before the fourth roll if it ends on roll 1, 2 or 3; these events are mutually exclusive with probabilities $\frac18$, $\frac78\times\frac18$ and $\left(\frac78\right)^2\times\frac18$.
answer.worked:
The game ends before the fourth roll exactly when the first $8$ occurs on roll $1$, $2$ or $3$. These are mutually exclusive.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{ends on roll }1) &= \frac18\\ P(\text{ends on roll }2) &= \frac78\times\frac18\\ P(\text{ends on roll }3) &= \frac78\times\frac78\times\frac18=\left(\frac78\right)^2\times\frac18\end{aligned}$$
Adding these probabilities,
$$P(\text{ends before roll }4)=\frac{1}{8} + \frac{7}{8} \times \frac{1}{8} + \left(\frac{7}{8}\right)^2 \times \frac{1}{8}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: What is the smallest value of $n$ for which the probability of the game ending before the $n$th roll is more than $\frac{3}{4}$?

answer.worked:
The game ends before roll $n$ if it ends on roll $1,2,\dots,n-1$, so the probability is a sum of $n-1$ terms.
$$P=\frac18+\frac78\times\frac18+\dots+\left(\frac78\right)^{n-2}\times\frac18$$
This is a geometric series with $a=\frac18$, $r=\frac78$ and $n-1$ terms.
$$\begin{aligned}P &= \frac{\frac18\left(1-\left(\frac78\right)^{n-1}\right)}{1-\frac78}\\ &= 1-\left(\frac78\right)^{n-1}\end{aligned}$$
We need $P>\frac34$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-\left(\tfrac78\right)^{n-1} &> \frac34\\ \left(\tfrac78\right)^{n-1} &< \frac14\\ (n-1)\ln\left(\tfrac78\right) &< \ln\left(\tfrac14\right)\\ n-1 &> \frac{\ln(0.25)}{\ln(0.875)}\quad(\text{since }\ln(0.875)<0)\\ n-1 &> 10.38\ldots\\ n &> 11.38\ldots\end{aligned}$$
Check: $\left(\frac78\right)^{10}\approx0.263>0.25$ but $\left(\frac78\right)^{11}\approx0.230<0.25$. The smallest integer is $n=12$.

content.prompt:
The 3rd, 4th, and 8th terms of an arithmetic sequence are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, $r\ne1$.
Find the numerical value of the common ratio for the sequence.

answer.worked:
Let the arithmetic sequence have first term $a$ and common difference $d$. A geometric sequence has a nonzero first term, so $T_3=a+2d\ne0$. Let $T_3=u$; then
$$\begin{aligned}T_3&=a+2d=u\\ T_4&=a+3d=ur\\ T_8&=a+7d=ur^2\end{aligned}$$
Since $T_4^2=u^2r^2=T_3T_8$ (no division needed):
$$\begin{aligned}(a+3d)^2&=(a+2d)(a+7d)\\ a^2+6ad+9d^2&=a^2+9ad+14d^2\\ 0&=3ad+5d^2\\ 0&=d(3a+5d)\end{aligned}$$
If $d=0$, all three terms are equal, so $r=1$, which is excluded. Hence $d\ne0$ and $3a+5d=0$, so $a=-\frac{5d}{3}$.

Then $T_3=a+2d=\frac d3\ne0$ (consistent with a nonzero first term) and $T_4=a+3d=\frac{4d}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\frac{T_4}{T_3}\\ &=\frac{\frac{4d}{3}}{\frac d3}\\ &=4\end{aligned}$$
Check: $T_8=a+7d=\frac{16d}{3}=4\times\frac{4d}{3}=T_4\,r$, as required.

classification.difficultyReason: Express selected AP terms as consecutive GP terms, connect unequal AP index gaps to the GP relation, and use the excluded ratio to resolve the algebra.

content.prompt:
Louis is playing a poker machine at his local club.
Each game on the poker machine is a Bernoulli trial where the probability of winning is $p$, with $0 < p < 1$.
Louis is determined to keep playing until he wins one game.
The random variable $X$ is the total number of games that Louis plays.
Thus $P(X=1)=p$, $P(X=2)=p(1-p)$, $P(X=3)=p(1-p)^2 \dots P(X=n)=p(1-p)^{n-1}$, where $n$ is a positive integer.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Show that the probability that Louis plays more than $n$ games is $(1-p)^n$.

answer.worked:
First, calculate the probability that Louis plays $n$ or fewer games, $P(X \leq n)$:
$$\begin{align*}
P(X \leq n) &= P(X=1) + P(X=2) + \dots + P(X=n) \\
&= p + p(1-p) + p(1-p)^2 + \dots + p(1-p)^{n-1}
\end{align*}$$
This is a geometric series with initial term $a = p$ and common ratio $r = 1-p$. The sum of the first $n$ terms is:
$$\begin{align*}
S_n &= \frac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r} \\
&= \frac{p(1 - (1-p)^n)}{1 - (1-p)} \\
&= \frac{p(1 - (1-p)^n)}{p} \\
&= 1 - (1-p)^n
\end{align*}$$
Using the complement rule:
$$\begin{align*}
P(X > n) &= 1 - P(X \leq n) \\
&= 1 - (1 - (1-p)^n) \\
&= (1-p)^n
\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: If $m$ and $n$ are two positive integers, show that $P(X > m+n | X > m) = P(X > n)$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt:
Louis thinks that he is "building up luck" by playing the same poker machine, even when he loses.
Explain why this notion is incorrect.

answer.short: His past losses do not affect his future probability of winning, so his luck does not "build up".
answer.worked: The result from $\textbf{(ii)}$ shows the distribution is memoryless. This means the probability of needing more than $n$ further games to win, given that he has already played and lost $m$ games, is exactly the same as if he were starting fresh. His past losses do not affect his future probability of winning, so his luck does not "build up".

content.prompt:
The first rows of Pascal’s triangle are shown below.
Consider an ordering of the numbers, counting down and across the rows, as given in the diagram.

Find the sum of the first 496 numbers of Pascal’s triangle.

answer.worked:
The number of entries in the first $n$ rows is $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n$.
$$\begin{align*}
1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n &= 496 \\
\frac{n(n+1)}{2} &= 496 \\
n(n+1) &= 992 \\
n^2 + n - 992 &= 0 \\
(n+32)(n-31) &= 0
\end{align*}$$
Since $n>0$, the first 496 numbers are exactly the first 31 rows.
The sum of the entries in row $k$ is $2^{k-1}$.
$$\begin{align*}
S &= 2^0 + 2^1 + 2^2 + \cdots + 2^{30} \\
&= \frac{2^{31}-1}{2-1} \\
&= 2^{31}-1 \\
&= 2\,147\,483\,647
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Aida has $\$500\,000$ in an investment account earning interest at a rate of $3\%$ per annum compounded annually.
At the end of the first year, Aida withdraws $\$25\,000$ for expenses.
Each subsequent year, the amount that Aida withdraws increases by $5\%$ due to rising expenses.
Let $A_n$ be the balance of Aida's investment account at the end of the $n$th year.

children.label: b
children.prompt: For how many complete years will Aida be able to withdraw money from this account in order to meet her expenses?

answer.worked:
Continuing the pattern, the subtracted bracket is a geometric series with $n$ terms, so
$$A_n=500\,000(1.03)^n-25\,000(1.03)^{n-1}\left[1+\frac{1.05}{1.03}+\cdots+\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^{n-1}\right]$$
The bracket has $a=1$, $r=\frac{1.05}{1.03}$, so it equals $\dfrac{\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n-1}{\frac{0.02}{1.03}}$.
Set $A_n=0$:
$$\begin{align*}500\,000(1.03)&=25\,000\times\frac{\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n-1}{\frac{0.02}{1.03}}\\20.6&=\frac{1.03\left(\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n-1\right)}{0.02}\\\left(\frac{1.05}{1.03}\right)^n&=1.4\\n&=\log_{\frac{1.05}{1.03}}1.4\\n&=17.49\ldots\end{align*}$$
The balance runs out during the 18th year, so Aida can withdraw for $17$ complete years.

$$e^{-\frac{n}{n-1}}<\left(1-\frac1n\right)^n<e^{-1}.$$

A game is being played by $n$ people, $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$, sitting around a table.
Each person has a card with their own name on it and all the cards are placed in a box in the middle of the table.
Each person in turn, starting with $A_1$, draws a card at random from the box.
If the person draws their own card, they win the game and the game ends.
Otherwise, the card is returned to the box and the next person draws a card at random.
The game continues until someone wins.
Let $W$ be the probability that $A_1$ wins the game.
Let $p = \frac{1}{n}$ and $q = 1 - \frac{1}{n}$.

answer.worked:
Player $A_1$ can win on their first attempt with probability $p$. If $A_1$ does not win on the first attempt (probability $q$), then all other $n-1$ players must also fail to win for $A_1$ to get another turn. The probability that all $n$ players fail to win in a given round is $q^n$. If this happens, the game effectively resets and it is $A_1$'s turn again, so the probability $A_1$ wins from this point onwards is $W$.
$$\begin{align*}
W &= p + q^n W
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer and let $W_m$ be the probability that $A_1$ wins in no more than $m$ attempts.
Use the source result from Question 8(b) to show that, if $n$ is large, $\frac{W_m}{W}$ is approximately equal to $1 - e^{-m}$.

entries.description: Geometric Sequences
A geometric sequence, also called a geometric progression or exponential sequence, is a sequence where there is a common ratio between each pair of consecutive terms.

The common ratio (r) is the same value that you multiply each term to get the next term. It can be:
• Greater than one (sequence increases, also called exponential growth)
• Between zero and one (sequence decreases, also called exponential decay)
• Negative (sequence alternates between positive and negative terms)

We check whether a sequence is geometric by finding the ratio between consecutive terms and seeing if they are constant.
\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}} = r
